questions.stem: Budgetary policy can help stabilise the business cycle because the government can:
options: direct the Reserve Bank to change its target for inflation each year
change its spending and taxation to influence aggregate demand
set the cash rate target and the interest rates charged by banks
fix the value of the Australian dollar against other major currencies
questions.explanation: The budget sets government spending and taxation, both of which affect total spending in the economy. The cash rate is set by the RBA as part of monetary policy.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a direct tax?
options: Excise on fuel
Customs duty on imports
Personal income tax
The goods and services tax
questions.explanation: A direct tax is levied on income and paid by the person or company that earns it. GST, excise and customs duty are indirect taxes on spending.

questions.stem: A progressive tax is one where:
options: the proportion of income paid in tax rises as income rises
every taxpayer pays the same proportion of their income in tax
the proportion of income paid in tax falls as income rises
all goods and services are taxed at the same rate when they are sold
questions.explanation: Under a progressive tax, higher earners pay a larger share of their income in tax. Australia's personal income tax, with rising marginal rates, is the main example.

questions.stem: The goods and services tax (GST) is regarded as a regressive tax because:
options: it is levied on household income rather than on spending, so low earners face a higher rate of tax
lower-income households spend a larger share of their income, so pay a larger share of it in GST
the rate of GST rises as a household's income rises
it applies only to luxury goods bought by high-income earners
questions.explanation: GST is charged at the same rate on spending, but lower-income households spend most of what they earn while higher-income households save more. As a share of income, the GST burden is therefore greater for those on low incomes.

questions.stem: A tax levied at a single flat rate on all taxable income, whatever the amount, is described as:
options: progressive
regressive
indirect
proportional
questions.explanation: A proportional tax takes the same percentage of income from everyone. A progressive tax takes a rising share as income rises, and a regressive tax takes a falling share.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a source of government revenue other than taxation?
options: Grants paid by the federal government to the states
Proceeds from the sale of a government-owned business
Unemployment benefits paid to people looking for work
Interest paid by the government on its bonds
questions.explanation: Governments also earn revenue from the dividends of government businesses and the sale of government assets. Benefits, interest payments and grants are expenses, not revenue.

questions.stem: A hypothetical income tax scale charges no tax on the first $20 000, 20 per cent on income from $20 001 to $60 000, and 35 per cent on income above $60 000. The tax on a taxable income of $80 000 is:
questions.explanation: Tax is 20 per cent of the $40 000 between $20 000 and $60 000, which is $8000, plus 35 per cent of the $20 000 above $60 000, which is $7000, a total of $15 000. Applying 35 per cent to the whole income gives $28 000, which ignores how marginal rates work.

questions.stem: Transfer payments are best described as:
options: payments by government for which no good or service is provided in return, such as the age pension
wages and salaries paid by government to the public servants who work in its departments and agencies
spending by government on long-lasting assets such as new roads, railways and hospitals
purchases of military equipment and other goods by government from private firms
questions.explanation: Transfer payments move income from taxpayers to recipients such as pensioners and job seekers, without any current production in return. Wages and asset purchases buy labour or goods, so they are current or capital expenditure.

questions.stem: Building a new railway line is classified as government:
options: current expenditure
transfer payment
indirect revenue
capital expenditure
questions.explanation: Capital expenditure is spending on long-lasting assets such as transport infrastructure. Current expenditure covers day-to-day running costs, such as wages.

questions.stem: Salaries paid to teachers in government schools are an example of government:
options: transfer payments
indirect taxation
current expenditure
capital expenditure
questions.explanation: Current expenditure covers the ongoing costs of providing government services, such as wages and consumables, within the year. Teachers provide a service in return for their pay, so their salaries are not transfer payments.

questions.stem: A budget deficit occurs when, over a financial year:
options: spending on imports exceeds export earnings
government expenses exceed government revenue
government revenue exceeds government expenses
government debt falls to zero
questions.explanation: A deficit is a shortfall of revenue relative to expenses over the year, which must be financed. A surplus is the reverse, and a balanced budget means revenue equals expenses.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical year, government receipts are $650 billion, payments are $680 billion and GDP is $2500 billion. The budget outcome as a proportion of GDP is:
options: a surplus of 1.2 per cent of GDP
a deficit of 4.6 per cent of GDP
a deficit of 3.0 per cent of GDP
a deficit of 1.2 per cent of GDP
questions.explanation: Payments exceed receipts by $30 billion, and 30 ÷ 2500 × 100 = 1.2 per cent of GDP, a deficit. Dividing by receipts instead of GDP gives about 4.6 per cent.

questions.stem: The underlying cash balance, the government's headline measure of the budget outcome, is based on:
options: the difference between the government's cash receipts and cash payments in a year
the total stock of Commonwealth government debt outstanding at the end of the financial year
the difference between the value of Australia's exports and imports in a year
the change in the RBA's cash rate target over the course of the financial year
questions.explanation: The underlying cash balance measures the gap between what the government receives and what it pays out over the year, with some adjustments. Government debt is a stock built up from past outcomes.

questions.stem: The budget outcome is often expressed as a proportion of GDP because this:
options: excludes the effect of automatic stabilisers, so only discretionary decisions remain
shows the deficit or surplus relative to the size of the economy, allowing comparison over time
removes the effect of transfer payments, so only spending on goods and services is counted in the outcome
converts the nominal outcome into a real outcome by removing the effect of inflation
questions.explanation: A deficit of a given dollar amount matters less in a larger economy, so scaling by GDP makes outcomes comparable across years and countries. It does not separate cyclical from structural changes.

questions.stem: The Australian Government most commonly finances a budget deficit by:
options: selling Australia's foreign exchange reserves held by the Reserve Bank
issuing government securities, such as bonds, to borrow from investors
asking the Reserve Bank to print money and lend it to the government directly
raising the cash rate so that it earns more interest on its deposits
questions.explanation: The government borrows by selling bonds to investors in Australia and overseas, adding to public debt. Printing money to fund the government directly is not how Australia finances its deficits.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a way of using a budget surplus?
options: Repaying existing government debt
Issuing new government bonds
Raising the RBA's cash rate target
Increasing the current account deficit
questions.explanation: A surplus can be used to repay debt or to build up government financial assets, such as investments in a sovereign wealth fund. Issuing bonds is a way of financing a deficit.

questions.stem: Successive budget deficits, financed by borrowing, will tend to:
options: reduce the level of government (public) debt
leave the level of government debt unchanged
reduce the government's interest payments
increase the level of government (public) debt
questions.explanation: Each deficit financed by borrowing adds to the stock of public debt. A larger debt also raises interest payments, which add to future expenses.

questions.stem: Higher government debt can constrain future budgets because:
options: it automatically raises the RBA's cash rate target by a set amount each year
all government debt must legally be repaid in full within one financial year
it directly reduces the income tax revenue collected from households
interest payments on the debt use revenue that could fund other spending
questions.explanation: Interest on government debt is an expense that must be paid before other priorities. As debt grows, interest takes up more of the budget, reducing room for spending or tax cuts.

questions.stem: Automatic stabilisers are:
options: budget items that change with the business cycle without any new government decision
deliberate changes to spending and taxation announced by the government in the budget
decisions by the Reserve Bank to change the cash rate target as conditions change
laws requiring the government to balance the budget in every financial year
questions.explanation: Tax receipts and welfare payments respond automatically to changes in incomes and unemployment. This is the cyclical component of the budget.

questions.stem: During a downturn, automatic stabilisers tend to:
options: require parliament to pass new laws raising unemployment benefits during the downturn
reduce tax receipts and raise welfare payments, cushioning the fall in aggregate demand
raise tax receipts and reduce welfare payments, reinforcing the fall in aggregate demand
push the budget towards surplus as the government cuts its spending to save money
questions.explanation: As incomes fall, less tax is collected, and as unemployment rises, more people receive benefits. Households keep more spending power than they otherwise would, which softens the downturn.

questions.stem: Progressive income tax acts as an automatic stabiliser because, during a boom:
options: tax receipts rise faster than incomes, restraining the growth of spending
parliament votes to raise the tax rates that apply to each income bracket
tax receipts fall, which adds further stimulus to aggregate demand
taxpayers move into lower tax brackets as their incomes grow
questions.explanation: As incomes rise, more income is taxed at higher marginal rates, so tax takes a growing share. That slows the growth of disposable income and spending without any change in tax law.

questions.stem: An economic slowdown pushes the budget from a small surplus into deficit, with no change in government policy. This change reflects:
options: a deliberate shift to a contractionary stance of budgetary policy
an increase in discretionary spending announced by the government
the cyclical component of the budget, through automatic stabilisers
the structural component of the budget, through discretionary decisions
questions.explanation: With no policy change, the budget moved only because tax receipts fell and welfare payments rose as the economy slowed. That is the cyclical component, driven by automatic stabilisers.

questions.stem: Discretionary stabilisers are:
options: changes in the RBA's cash rate target
deliberate changes in government spending or taxation made to influence aggregate demand
changes in tax receipts and welfare payments that happen automatically over the business cycle
unemployment benefits paid to people who lose their jobs in a downturn
questions.explanation: Discretionary measures are new policy decisions, such as tax cuts or spending programs, and make up the structural component of the budget. Automatic changes over the cycle are the cyclical component.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a discretionary budget measure?
options: Rising income tax receipts as wages grow during an expansion
A new one-off cash payment to low-income households announced in the budget
Higher unemployment benefit payments as more people lose their jobs
Lower company tax receipts as business profits fall in a downturn
questions.explanation: A newly announced payment is a deliberate policy decision, so it is discretionary. The other changes happen automatically as economic conditions change.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical year, the budget moves from a deficit of $20 billion to a deficit of $35 billion. Automatic stabilisers account for $10 billion of the deterioration. The discretionary (structural) change is:
options: a $5 billion improvement, indicating a contractionary stance
a $25 billion deterioration, indicating a contractionary stance
a $5 billion deterioration, indicating an expansionary stance
a $15 billion deterioration, indicating an expansionary stance
questions.explanation: The total deterioration is $15 billion, of which $10 billion is cyclical, leaving $5 billion from discretionary decisions. A discretionary move towards a larger deficit adds to aggregate demand, so the stance is expansionary.

questions.stem: In a strong boom with no new policy decisions, the budget outcome and public debt would tend to:
options: improve, with debt growing more slowly or falling
worsen, with debt rising more quickly
improve, while debt rises more quickly
worsen, while debt falls more quickly
questions.explanation: In a boom, tax receipts rise and welfare payments fall automatically, so the budget improves. A smaller deficit or a surplus means less borrowing, so debt grows more slowly or is repaid.

questions.stem: The government announces large new infrastructure spending during a recession, while automatic stabilisers are also operating. The most likely effect on the budget is:
options: a larger deficit and higher public debt
a smaller deficit and lower public debt
a move into surplus as the economy recovers
no change in debt, as this is capital spending
questions.explanation: Both the cyclical component, through falling receipts and rising benefits, and the discretionary spending increase the deficit. The extra borrowing adds to public debt, whether the spending is current or capital.

questions.stem: An expansionary budgetary policy stance means the government is:
options: asking the RBA to raise the cash rate to slow spending
using discretionary measures that add to aggregate demand
cutting its spending and raising taxes to reduce aggregate demand
keeping revenue exactly equal to expenses in every year
questions.explanation: An expansionary stance uses tax cuts or spending increases to stimulate demand, moving the structural budget towards deficit. Cutting spending and raising taxes is a contractionary stance.

questions.stem: Why is the overall budget outcome not a reliable guide to the stance of budgetary policy?
options: It excludes the government's spending on capital projects such as roads, railways and hospitals
It is measured in real terms rather than in nominal terms, so it hides the effect of inflation
It is determined by the Reserve Bank rather than by the government's own budget decisions
It includes cyclical changes from automatic stabilisers, which do not reflect discretionary decisions
questions.explanation: The budget can move into deficit simply because the economy has slowed, even if the government has tightened policy. The stance is judged from the structural component, which reflects deliberate decisions.

questions.stem: The budget moves from a deficit of 2 per cent of GDP to a deficit of 1 per cent of GDP, entirely because of discretionary tax increases and spending cuts. The budget stance is:
options: neutral, as the budget is still not balanced
expansionary, as public debt is still rising
contractionary, as discretionary changes reduce aggregate demand
expansionary, as the budget remains in deficit
questions.explanation: The stance depends on the direction of the discretionary change, not on whether the budget is in deficit. Raising taxes and cutting spending take demand out of the economy, which is contractionary.

questions.stem: A contractionary budget stance is most appropriate when:
options: the economy is in a recession and confidence is weak
prices are falling and firms have spare capacity
aggregate demand is growing too fast and inflation is above target
unemployment is rising and inflation is below the target band
questions.explanation: When demand is outstripping capacity, cutting spending or raising taxes slows the growth of aggregate demand and eases inflation. Weak demand calls for an expansionary stance.

questions.stem: Increased government spending on public hospitals can raise living standards because it:
options: raises interest rates for savers by increasing the government's demand for borrowed funds
improves access to health care, a non-material living standard, and adds to aggregate demand
reduces public debt by lowering the interest the government pays on its existing borrowings each year
lowers the participation rate as more workers are able to retire early from the workforce
questions.explanation: Better health services improve wellbeing directly, and the spending also creates jobs and income. On its own, extra spending does not reduce public debt.

questions.stem: The government runs an expansionary budget while the RBA is trying to bring inflation down. The likely problem is that:
options: inflation will fall faster, as both policies reduce aggregate demand at the same time
the exchange rate will become fixed, as the RBA can no longer change the cash rate
aggregate supply will fall, as government spending replaces private production
the two policies work against each other, so interest rates may need to rise further
questions.explanation: Extra government spending adds to demand while higher interest rates aim to reduce it, so each policy offsets part of the other. The RBA may have to raise rates by more to reach its inflation target.

questions.stem: A strength of budgetary policy compared with monetary policy is that it can:
options: be targeted at particular groups, regions or industries
be changed quickly at any meeting without needing legislation
be used without any effect on the level of public debt
be decided free of any political pressures
questions.explanation: The government can direct spending or tax changes to the people, places or industries that need them, such as a struggling region. Monetary policy affects the whole economy at once.

questions.stem: A strength of automatic stabilisers is that they:
options: can be targeted at a single industry or region that is going through a downturn
keep the budget balanced in every financial year, whatever the economic conditions happen to be
raise the economy's productive capacity by funding long-term infrastructure projects
respond straight away to changes in economic conditions, without new decisions or laws
questions.explanation: Because tax receipts and welfare payments respond on their own as incomes and jobs change, there is no implementation lag. They cushion the cycle but do not keep the budget balanced.

questions.stem: A strength of direct government spending as a stabiliser is that it:
options: adds directly to aggregate demand, rather than relying on households and firms to borrow
has no implementation lag, since every spending decision takes effect on the day it is announced
never adds to public debt, because it is always funded from existing tax revenue
is set by the RBA, so it is free of political pressures
questions.explanation: Government spending is itself part of aggregate demand, so it raises demand even when households and firms are unwilling to borrow and spend. Monetary policy relies on private borrowing responding to lower rates.

questions.stem: A weakness of discretionary budgetary policy is its implementation lag, which means that:
options: it cannot affect aggregate demand at all unless the RBA also changes the cash rate
only the Reserve Bank can approve a change in government spending or taxation
changes must be planned, legislated and put into effect, which can take many months
its effects on aggregate demand wear off within a few days of a change being made by parliament
questions.explanation: Discretionary measures usually need legislation and time to set up programs, so stimulus may arrive after the economy has already turned. Automatic stabilisers avoid this lag.

questions.stem: Discretionary budgetary policy may be poorly timed or poorly judged because:
options: the Reserve Bank must approve every budget before the Treasurer can present it to federal parliament
automatic stabilisers prevent the government from making any discretionary changes
tax rates are fixed by the Constitution and cannot be changed by parliament
political pressures can make governments reluctant to cut spending or raise taxes in a boom
questions.explanation: Contractionary measures are unpopular, so governments may delay them even when the economy is overheating. This political constraint is one reason monetary policy is set by an independent RBA.

questions.stem: Large government borrowing to fund a deficit may weaken the effect of budgetary policy because:
options: it lowers interest rates and encourages too much private borrowing, known as crowding in
it reduces the level of public debt, so the government must cut its spending later
it lowers tax revenue directly, so the deficit grows by more than the spending increase
it can push up interest rates and reduce private investment, known as crowding out
questions.explanation: Heavy government borrowing competes with private borrowers for funds, which can raise interest rates and discourage private investment. Some of the boost from government spending is then offset by lower private spending.

questions.stem: Persistent structural budget deficits are a concern mainly because they:
options: disappear automatically once the economy recovers from a downturn
are caused by automatic stabilisers that cannot be changed by government
reduce aggregate demand during booms, making expansions shorter
add to public debt and interest costs even when the economy is operating strongly
questions.explanation: A structural deficit remains even at full employment, so debt keeps rising through the whole cycle. That leaves less room to respond to the next downturn; cyclical deficits, by contrast, shrink as the economy recovers.
